name: The Chimney That Ducks

severity_by_style.why: The stacks read against the sky as the terminating verticals of a symmetrical composition; ducked, the roof has no incident at all.
The regional minimum is 6 ft above the ridge because the stacks are at the gable ends.
3 ft above the ridge minimum, and the stack is a principal vertical.
Broad, low and heavy on purpose; heightening it would break the horizontal datum.

symptom: A chimney that clears the ridge by a foot or less, or one on a slope whose top stops below the ridge line altogether. It reads as a lump interrupting the roof rather than as the vertical that terminates the composition.

cause.explanation: IRC R1003.9 is a minimum - 3 ft above the roof penetration and 2 ft above anything within 10 ft - and both the mason and the builder read a minimum as a target. Every foot of stack above the roof is unbraced masonry that has to be designed for wind and, in much of the country, for seismic; it costs $150-400 a foot; and it is the roof's single largest flashing and maintenance liability. Three separate pressures all push the same way, and none of them is aesthetic.
cause.cost_saved: $500-2,000 per stack, plus a structural detail.

rule_violated.statement: 24-120 in above the ridge; the Chesapeake and Low Country minimum is 72 in.
Chimney breadth at least 1/6 of the elevation it sits on; stack height at least 3 ft above the ridge.
Not less than 3 ft above the highest point where the chimney passes through the roof, and not less than 2 ft higher than any portion of the building within 10 ft.

correct_practice: The code figure is a draft and safety rule, not a proportional one, and the two answer different questions. Historically the stack is a compositional element: on a Georgian house 2 to 10 ft above the ridge, with the Chesapeake and Low Country minimum at 6 ft, because the stacks stand at the gable ends where they must read against the sky as the terminating verticals of a symmetrical composition. On a Tudor Revival house the stack is at least 3 ft above the ridge and at least a sixth of the elevation's width in breadth. The rule of thumb that resolves most cases: an end-wall stack should be tall enough that its top clears a line continuing the roof slope past the ridge, so that it reads as taller than the roof rather than as an interruption of it.

fixes.right: Design the stack height from the elevation and check it against the code, not the other way round.
fixes.cheap: Two or three feet of additional brick at $150-400 a foot, decided at the drawing stage. If height cannot be had, get BREADTH instead: a stack 32 in wide at 30 in above the ridge reads far better than one 20 in wide at 48 in, because the eye judges a chimney's presence from its silhouette area, not its height alone.
fixes.dishonest: A tall decorative pot or shroud added to a short stack. The pot is a real traditional element with real proportions of its own, and a 30 in pot on a 24 in stack reads as a chimney wearing a hat two sizes too big.

test.note: Traditional work runs 0.25-0.5. Under 0.15 the chimney has ducked. A stack whose top falls below the ridge line in the image fails immediately.

secondary_tests.note: The code floor, which is a draught and safety rule and not a proportional one - and which everyone reads as a target. Also 2 ft above anything within 10 ft.
The compensating measurement. The eye judges a chimney's presence from silhouette area, so a stack 32 in wide at 30 in above the ridge reads better than one 20 in wide at 48 in.

detection: Measure, in a gable-end or oblique photograph, the height of the stack above the ridge as a fraction of the roof's eave-to-ridge height. Under 0.15 the chimney has ducked; traditional work runs 0.25-0.5. A stack whose top falls below the ridge line in the image fails immediately. Second check: stack width against stack height above the roof - a stack visibly wider than it is tall above the roof is a chase or a very shy chimney.

exceptions.why: The chimney is broad, low and heavy on purpose - the fattest object in the composition - and heightening it would break the horizontal datum the whole style is built on.
exceptions.bounds: It has to earn the low height with breadth: 30-48 in of visible face, and it must still be the visually heaviest element on the building.

bounds_test.note: It has to earn the low height with breadth, and must still be the visually heaviest element on the building.

exceptions.why: A clinker-brick or boulder stack is deliberately squat and massive, part of the stacked-material logic of base, wall and gable.
exceptions.bounds: Breadth and material weight must do the work; a narrow squat stack is just short.

bounds_test.note: Breadth and material weight must do the work; a narrow squat stack is just short.

exceptions.why: A central stack on a Cape sits close over a ridge that is only 18-22 ft above grade, and it is broad rather than tall.
exceptions.bounds: Still 24 in minimum above the ridge, and 30 in or more wide - the Cape's stack is a massive object seen against a low roof.

bounds_test.note: And 30 in or more wide - the Cape's stack is a massive object seen against a low roof only 18-22 ft above grade.

exceptions.why: A stucco chimney terminated with a small tile-capped hood is deliberately squat and sculptural.
exceptions.bounds: The termination must be a shaped hood or a tile cap; a flat stucco box stopping short is still the fault.

bounds_test.note: The termination must be a shaped hood or a tile cap; a flat stucco box stopping short is still the fault.

inverted_by.statement: A tall stack is the fault. The chimney must be the fattest and heaviest object in the composition and must not rise far enough to break the horizontal banding.
A slender tall stack is the fault; the mass belongs in the base.
A tall brick stack is the fault; the chimney is a squat sculptural stucco form with a tile-capped hood.

confused_with.difference: That fault is the top 18 in of a stack of adequate height. This one is the height itself.
